title: Digital Cognitive Test Battery
summary: With Beit Rivka, we turn traditional pen-and-paper cognitive tests into tablet tests with automatic scoring: clock drawing, HITBER, memory, orientation and a virtual supermarket.
description:
Cognitive assessment still relies mostly on paper, pen and a stopwatch. That causes three problems:

- **Inefficiency** — a senior staff member must supervise the whole session.
- **Lost information** — the test itself (for example the clock drawing) is usually not kept in the medical record; only the score is.
- **Subjectivity** — manual scoring depends on interpretation, so the same patient may get different scores from different assessors.

In collaboration with **Beit Rivka**, we are building a digital battery that runs on tablets, stores every result securely, and scores automatically.

## The tests

### Clock Drawing Test (CDT)
Our first two versions taught us a lot. The first interface was too complex: patients failed on operating the app, not on cognition. The second was oversimplified and moved too far from the original test. The current version follows the original protocol closely:
1. **Drawing** — the patient draws a clock on the tablet, places the numbers, and sets the hands to 11:10.
2. **Comprehension** — a ready-made clock is shown, and the patient resets it according to an instruction that requires a calculation.

### HITBER
A new digital test based on the Mini-Mental, designed for tablets. Classic tasks such as free writing, complex drawing and serial subtraction are replaced with interactive tasks scored by an algorithm. No typing or voice recognition is needed; clear instructions and predefined choices keep it simple for older adults.

### Memory test
The test assesses visual-spatial memory under load. Patients first place objects in rooms of their choice. After a short distraction, they recall the locations while new "distractor" objects appear. A diary-planning task then adds executive load before a final recall.

### Orientation test
Sometimes a low score reflects unfamiliarity with tablets rather than cognitive decline. This short "entry gate" asks for about seven very simple actions (dragging a shape, drawing a line, pressing buttons) to confirm the patient can operate the device before the main tests.

### Supermarket test
This test assesses orientation, attention, memory and multitasking in an everyday setting. The patient picks a recipe and collects its ingredients from a moving conveyor. Then they shop for two lists on a budget in a virtual supermarket, dealing with out-of-stock items, last-minute requests and pop-up ads.

## Status
The clock and HITBER tests completed **two rounds of clinical trials with more than 100 patients**. The memory and orientation tests completed a trial with **more than 50 patients**. Both included a pilot at Protea in the Village. The tests can be deployed now through [DMT – Proms++](/projects/dmt-proms), and the next phase will take them into the community.

## Vision: one unified battery
All results sync securely to a server and a management system with table and graph views. The goal is a single, adaptive battery: it starts with orientation, and real-time scoring routes the patient to the next module, so the whole process feels like one smooth test.
